purpose: Rolapitant is used to help prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy (cancer treatment). It is especially helpful for preventing the nausea that can happen 24 hours or more after your chemo treatment, which is called delayed nausea. It is always used together with other anti-nausea medicines, not alone.
how_it_works: Your body releases a natural chemical called substance P during chemotherapy, which can trigger nausea and vomiting. Rolapitant works by blocking the receptor that substance P attaches to in your brain, so the signal to feel nauseated is reduced. Think of it like putting a lock on a door so the nausea trigger cannot get in.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include decreased appetite, hiccups, dizziness, indigestion or upset stomach, and low white blood cell counts (neutropenia). Some people may also feel tired or have abdominal pain.
warnings: Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, because rolapitant can interact with many drugs and cause serious problems, including affecting how your heart beats. It should not be used more than once every 2 weeks. Let your doctor know if you have liver problems. Avoid taking thioridazine (an antipsychotic) while using this medicine, as it can cause a dangerous heart rhythm. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is one 180 mg tablet taken by mouth within 2 hours before your chemotherapy session. It is only taken once per chemo cycle, and your doctor will combine it with other anti-nausea medicines for the best protection.
